title: How to Safely Stop Antidepressants: A Tapering Guide
description: Coming off antidepressants requires careful tapering. How to do it safely, what withdrawal feels like, when you're ready, and what to watch for.

content.text: Stopping antidepressants too quickly can cause withdrawal symptoms. Here's how to taper safely and what to expect.
Antidepressants cause your brain to adapt. Stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation syndrome—not because you're addicted, but because your brain needs time to readjust.
Never stop antidepressants cold turkey. Always taper under medical supervision.
Symptoms typically start 2-4 days after stopping or reducing, peak around day 5, and resolve within 1-3 weeks.

items: You've been well for at least 6-12 months
You're in a stable life situation (not during major stress)
You have support systems in place
You've discussed it with your prescriber
You have a plan for monitoring relapse
If symptoms are bad, stay at current dose longer

content.text: Some people need slower tapers lasting 6-12 months. Listen to your body.
For very gradual tapers, liquid formulations allow precise dose reductions. Ask your doctor about this option.
It can be hard to distinguish:

items: Starts within days of dose reduction
Starts weeks to months after stopping

content.text: Some people experience prolonged withdrawal or relapse every time they try to stop. This is okay. Staying on medication long-term is a valid choice if it's helping you function.

Stopping antidepressants requires patience and medical supervision. Taper slowly, expect some discomfort, and have a plan for monitoring your mood. If you've tried and struggled, know that long-term use is safe for most people.
